title: US and Denmark Strike Greenland Security Deal, Ending Months of Tension
summary:
The US and Denmark announced a deal on Greenland's security on Saturday, resolving a diplomatic dispute sparked by President Donald Trump's threats to seize the semi-autonomous Danish territory by force.

Trump said Denmark would grant the US "permanent control over security, and all other needs" in Greenland, a vast Arctic island. In a post on Truth Social, he said the deal came with "no cost to the United States" and included a rule that no US adversary could maintain a military presence in Greenland or "make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval."

The leaders of Denmark and Greenland welcomed the deal to "strengthen security," saying it was expected to be signed next week at the UN General Assembly. But they did not outline its contents, and no text of the agreement has been released.

Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said she was "pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement" for all three parties. In a joint statement with Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen, she said the deal "strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area" while also recognizing "the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination." Nielsen said the agreement "recognises Greenland's interests and our place in international co-operation."

Nato welcomed the deal. A spokesperson said it would "help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region." French President Emmanuel Macron said the deal helped "reaffirm Danish sovereignty" over the island. "I simply note that Danish sovereignty is respected, that international law is respected, and that this is what we were asking for," he said.

Trump had tried for months to purchase or annex Greenland, arguing it was vulnerable to adversaries including Russia and China. His repeated demands prompted an outcry from Greenlanders, Danes, and other Nato members. US Vice-President JD Vance toured a US military base in Greenland earlier this year, a visit viewed by Copenhagen and Nuuk as a provocation.

There is hope the crisis has now ended. Some Danish media interpreted the agreement as a quiet but significant triumph for Danish diplomacy. "Don't tell Trump that it's the Kingdom of Denmark that has won," read one headline in the newspaper Berlingske on Saturday.
why_it_matters: This episode shows how Arctic security — reshaped by melting ice, new shipping routes and great-power rivalry — is negotiated through alliances, treaties and international law rather than force, and how a small territory like Greenland tries to keep its own voice in decisions about its future.

background_read: Greenland is the world's largest island and an autonomous territory inside the Kingdom of Denmark: it runs most of its own affairs through its own parliament in Nuuk, while Denmark handles defence and foreign policy for the Kingdom.

Its position between North America and Europe, plus its minerals and newly opening shipping routes as Arctic ice melts, make it strategically valuable — the US has kept a military base in northwestern Greenland under a defence agreement reached in the 1950s.

Nato (the North Atlantic Treaty Organization — a military alliance of the United States, Denmark and about 30 other countries) welcomed the deal, since Greenland sits on the shortest route between Russia and North America.

Donald Trump (the US president since 2025) first floated buying Greenland during his first term, and US Vice-President JD Vance toured a US base on the island earlier this year, a visit Copenhagen and Nuuk saw as a provocation.

The UN General Assembly (the annual meeting where leaders of nearly every country speak in New York) is where the deal is expected to be signed next week — a setting that lets both sides present it as a diplomatic win.

perspectives.description: Washington gets security guarantees and a veto over rival activity, while Denmark and Greenland say their sovereignty, territorial integrity and right to self-determination are recognised. Nato and France read the outcome as a stabilising, rules-based result.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — Danes, Greenlanders and some allies
perspectives.description: Months of US pressure — including talk of seizing or annexing the island and Vance's base visit — caused outcry and was seen in Copenhagen and Nuuk as a provocation. No text has been released, so critics warn the terms could still hand Washington lasting control over Greenland's security choices.

Great-power interest in Greenland is not new: the US has maintained a base there since the Cold War because of its location on the shortest route between North America and Europe. Smaller states typically answer such pressure by anchoring their position in alliances and international law.

The real test is the signed text: how much say Greenland's own government keeps, and whether the agreement settles the issue or becomes a precedent for future US demands. Greenland's growing independence movement will also shape how the deal is received locally.
